Two-dimensional artificial electrical structures, or metasurfaces, that make up a
double-layered artificial structure or metametastructure can guide line waves
along their edge while preventing leakage into the surrounding area. This can be
accomplished by utilizing a type of local resonance within the structure. A
specific configuration consisting of an L-shaped split ring resonance and a cross
shaped element can transform weakly guided line waves into highly guided ones.
This modification can significantly enhance light interaction within the system.
Transforming a deflector that normally guides light sideways into one that can
guide light head-on is possible with a type of negative impedance conversion
when the structure is modified. This type of transformation can significantly
enhance the modulation depth of the resulting light signal by a factor of 20.

The standard SQL does not support recursive queries, which are necessary when working with hierarchical data, and thus SQL extensions have been developed to fill this gap. This research fully examines the complexity of answering a recursive queries under different constraints, and specifically focuses on two types of queries: those limited to $k$ levels and those defined by triple patterns with a cyclic dependency. The study provides detailed complexity results for both limited and unrestricted variants of these queries.

This research focuses on developing a runtime system that allows REX (Regular Expression Translator) to utilize the outcomes of regular expressions, utilizing an adaptive regular function utilizing finite state transducers (FST) and DFA. By utilizing FST or DFA as its underlying mechanism, this system can efficiently leverage regular expression results in situations involving infinite sequences, such as stream processing and software testing. In doing so, it can dynamically update its internal state based on newly acquired information, ensuring coinduction. This system is made accessible via the Web API and can be integrated with high-level programming languages. Furthermore, it can be utilized for learning probability distributions over text n-grams, leveraging a FST based regular expression translator (REx). This system was implemented in C, with the outcomes of the integration demonstrated in a prototype using the Web API and a LATEX parser example, with the code available on GitHub.

Using the available data from Belle and Belle II, this study thoroughly investigates the production of $K^{*0}\bar{K}^*0$ pairs in reactions $B^0 \to K^{*0}\bar{K}^*0$ at collision accelerators. To better understand these processes, theoretical predictions are made with specific models, notably the perturbative and non-perturbative components of Quantum Chromodynamics, while considering the effects of final state interactions through the $S$-wave approximation. The analysis predicts the observed discrepancies between the experiments and finds the probability of the $B^0 \to K^{*0}\bar{K}^*0$ reaction occurring at a specific time after its creation. This prediction can be utilized by experimental teams to identify and study this reaction more effectively.

In the context of statistical mechanics, a coexisting charge pattern is a phenomenon where positive and negative charges interact to form clusters that are concealed from view. These concealed clusters are called "hidden order" systems and they display a charge pattern where some charges aid in the detection of other clusters, while some remain invisible. Using machine learning, we are able to identify and evaluate the complexity of hidden order systems by training models on different configurations. When a model is able to accurately differentiate between clustered and random distributions of charges with a minimal amount of data, it is indicated that the coexisting charge pattern possesses a level of organization. Furthermore, we are able to refine a class of models called erasure transformers to successfully assess the entropy of charge patterns, while being able to outperform random models in evaluating concealed order patterns. Unlike regular models that are biased towards certain patterns, our refined model is able to accurately assess these hidden order systems.

A Kothare and Mitra average absolute deviation (AAD) measure of location centrality is introduced, being straightforward to calculate and user-friendly, centered around the midpoint of a probability distribution's spread. The expectation of AAD is employed to create a location estimator in both parametric and non-parametric contexts. The large sample behavior and consistency of the AAD estimator, in independent and identically distributed samples, are proven. Additionally, an asymptotically unbiased estimator is derived based on the covariance matrix of a multivariate AAD estimator, given independent multivariate data. Convergence rates in the mean square sense are established for both AAD and its expected value, enabling location and centrality assessment for non-parametric distributions. Furthermore, data transformation techniques using the Box-Tiao and Geometric Average spreading deviation are explored to aid in data analysis.

This study introduces an innovative approach to determine a second-order attainable set associated with the optimal control problem, which incorporates state constraints and applies to materials exhibiting the Magneto-Electric Hysteresis Effect. By leveraging the L2 continuity of the optimal control and the resulting smoothness in the attainable set boundary, we modify an existing first-order Variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equation, which was previously shown to have no solution due to the abrupt changes in the system dynamics, and prove that it accurately describes the boundary of the attainable set. Moreover, we demonstrate that it can be used to derive an infinite horizon state-constrained time-optimal control problem whose solution provides an answer to the problem at hand.

Current deep learning models rely on strong prior assumptions, such as symmetry and invariance, to generate efficient local representations. However, these representations often lack universality due to their reliance on specific task-related properties. In contrast, the natural visual system produces a highly versatile, modulated cyclical activation pattern that adapts to various contexts and performs exceptionally well in electroencephalography (EEG) stimulus recognition tasks. This natural representation is context-sensitive, cyclic, and efficiently uses a limited number of neural populations to encode a vast range of objects. Drawing from the principles of natural selection and adopting a continuous, optimization-based approach, we develop a new network that learns a context-sensitive cyclical representation through random mutations and selective pressures. Notably, this network does not require explicit training, allows for the exploration of multiple hyperparameter pressures, and achieves a highly efficient low-dimensional context representation when visual cycles are introduced. Furthermore, this low-dimensional representation demonstrates remarkable universality, outperforming established local representations in both accuracy and transferability when used for object classification.

The underlying mechanism of the brain's ventral temporal stream's ability to quickly recognize vital objects, like people, among a sea of other things, remains not fully understood. Recent research has shown that neurons in the occipital face area and parts of the ventral temporal cortex are specially tuned to differentiate objects by how 'alive' they are. This study seeks to uncover the core arrangement of 'alive' and 'not alive' preferences of these face-selective and object-selective neurons using methods from statistical physics. The findings indicate that there is a distinct pattern of organization within this arrangement, where 'people' and 'objects' categories are clearly separated. Furthermore, this research implies that a group of neurons with broader tuning could be added to improve the separation of categories without disrupting the current balance. The findings are presented at a conference in Pasadena, California, in December 2023.

This research is centered on efficient quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) for a specific class of functions, the Hecke-Maass newforms within $GL(3)$, and utilizes this focus to research the effective nonvanishing and the Landau-Siegel conjecture. We make a crucial assumption regarding the uniform distribution of the normalized Hecke eigenvalues for $GL(3)$ newforms. Under this assumption and under an additional technical condition, we derive two main consequences. First, given a newform $f$ and its associated L-function $L(s,f)$, under the effective nonnegativity of normalized Hecke eigenvalues, we derive an initial effective bound for the zero-free region of $L(s,f)$ and thereby an initial effective bound for the zero-free region near the critical line. Second, given any test function $\phi$ in a relevant class and its associated spectral newform $f_\phi$, if $f_\phi$ is of Rankin-Selberg type and has normalized eigenvalues that are effectively nonnegative, we derive an initial effective bound for the critical exponent of the family of $GL(3)$ L-functions in a relevant family, and thereby a relevant effective bound for the critical line. We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that extends a prior framework by incorporating anticipations and quantified relations. This expansion enables reasoning about program optimizations, side effects, higher-order relations, and existentially quantified variables. To validate our theory, we have provided examples of optimizations and variables in programs that manipulate quantum states. Our approach builds on the F* language, which already includes support for classical and higher-order relations and existential variables. Consequently, our implementation can utilize existing optimizations and program analyses in the K* verifier.

The COVID-19 epidemic has highlighted the crucial role of super-spreading events, which are responsible for a significant proportion of all cases. In many diseases and contexts, one individual accounts for more than 50 per cent of all cases. Traditional mathematical models, such as the SIR model, which assume homogeneous mixing, underestimate the number of cases in real-world epidemics. A more accurate model is required, one that takes into consideration the impact of super-spreading events. We propose a novel, minimal extension to the standard SIR model and derive the corresponding differential equations. This model allows us to analyse the long-term behaviour and obtain the explicit form of the equation of state. A numerical analysis, both for the new model and the standard SIR model, reveals that the probability of cases declining follows the long-term behaviour of the equation of state. Comparing the outcomes of the two models, we find that the inclusion of super-spreading events significantly increases the probability of epidemic survival. A simple rescaling of the standard SIR model's equations enables us to match the numerical outcomes of our new model. Ultimately, super-spreading events have a profound effect on the long-term behaviour of epidemics and cannot be overlooked.

This study defines and examines the codiskcyclic property in operators within complex Banach spaces, simultaneously expanding the concepts of diskcyclicity and supercyclicity. We establish codiskcyclicity for the shift operator and its adjoint, and provide a codiskcyclicity result for compact operators.

This research aims at identifying and reducing preprocessing bias in solar vector magnetic field measurements, a problem exacerbated by the increasing use of automatic processing. We have analyzed the performance of various methods for recognizing bias by examining the properties of linear correlations and coherence between the derived measurements and a reference set of low-noise measurements. A key finding from our study is that coherence effectively captures both random and systematic deviations caused by bias. To address the issue of bias, we have tested multiple approaches to minimize it, employing a coherence-based optimization framework. Notably, our results indicate that bilateral weighting is particularly effective in reducing bias, outperforming alternative methods such as circular regression, maximum likelihood estimation, and least-squares fitting. We have also discovered that coherence can serve as a useful metric for assessing the reliability of magnetic field measurements, enabling the creation of quality control maps that reflect their characteristics. These control maps generated by our approach exhibit significant coherence with those produced by the reference low-noise measurements, demonstrating the effectiveness of our bias recognition and alleviation methods.

Researchers studied several catalogs of young stars in the Milky Way, Milky Way neighbors, and further galaxies, including the Milky Way's molecular clouds, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, and the star-forming regions of nearby galaxies like M100, M61, and Coma Berenices. Statistical analysis revealed that spaces containing these stars behave similarly in our galaxy but appear more extended in extragalactic studies. Within our galaxy, most regions have a diameter of about 100 light years, whereas extragalactic studies showed significantly larger dimensions, potentially influenced by observational limitations and the scale of galaxies being studied.

We present an original approach to calculate the decay of charm quark pairs bound by weak forces into two virtual photons that further decay into any charge carrier. The proposed approach uses effective field theory to derive an order-specific operator connecting to the effective theory of heavy quark pairs. By combining this with the "potential non-local" approach, we can estimate the lattice QCD calculation for the charm-quark pair decay to two photons. This method may also be applicable to other decays such as hadronic radiative decays and lattice QCD calculations of form factors in heavy quark systems.

Solving the Hubbard model through Monte Carlo methods experiences the dreaded sign dilemma, causing Monte Carlo waves to oscillate wildly, which severely restricts the accuracy of the solution. This issue can be mitigated by employing complex-valued neural networks, allowing for the representation of the Hubbard wave function within a single training session. Introducing a new type of network called the complex multi-layer perceptron (CMLP), our results show that it outperforms the traditional MLML elapsing the sign dilemma of the Hubbard solver even with a minimal number of parameters.

Recently, a new concept called fragile integers has been introduced, which are integers that significantly diverge from their natural predecessors. We have made the first analytical progress on this topic by focusing on a specific group of fragile integers denoted as $\mathcal{F}$, which are those with a moderate divergence. In this study, we have determined the density of $\mathcal{F}$ among integers with a given size and found that it relates to the Dickman $\rho$ function. Specifically, we have found that the density is equal to the difference between 1 and the value of the Dickman function at 2, which approximates to 0.306 when evaluated numerically. Furthermore, we have obtained exact asymptotic estimates for various properties of integers in $\mathcal{F}$, including their average values for the omega function, the Bashashat function, and the density of prime numbers.

Given any non-empty free monoid $\Sigma^*$, we investigate how topological entropy and factor complexity interact with the application of free monoid homomorphisms, provided the images of the basis elements $\Sigma$ are also considered as the basis of another free monoid. This study builds on earlier work by Masseroli and Recchioni and extends the initial observations by Rozenberg and Westerbaan. Our analysis reveals that the entropy of the image language $\phi(L)$ relates to the entropy of the original language $\Sigma$ and a auxiliary context-sensitive language $K_\phi$, specific to the monoid mapping $\phi$. Similarly, the complexity of the image word $|\phi(u)|$ has a connection to the complexity of the original word $u$ and $K_\phi$. Notably, if $K_\phi$ has low complexity, the entropy and complexity of the image are directly proportional to those of the original. Conversely, in most cases, the relationship between the entropy or complexity of the image and the original language/word involves a more nuanced, non-linear connection.

By leveraging previously acquired knowledge, the strategy of zero-shot task adaptation enables a model to generalize beyond its training experiences, making it essential for building robust models in the realm of zero-shot task generalization. Despite the promising concept, the implementation of zero-shot task generalization is a complex challenge due to the lack of data for new, untested tasks. To tackle this issue, we've designed an unsupervised approach that employs retrieval enhancement to facilitate cross-task learning. Our framework starts by training separate autoencoders for each known task to capture their unique data patterns. Upon the model encounters an untested task, it uses the trained components to adapt without needing additional training. We've conducted comprehensive experiments on a comprehensive dataset consisting of multiple tasks, and our results show significant performance gains due to the unsupervised cross-task learning improvement.

This paper introduces the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm, an innovative approach for rapidly
calculating autonomous factor analyses in a limited time window. It achieves this
efficiency by utilizing an approximate method based on a linearized version of the
covariance matrix. A key benefit of the algorithm is its suitability for real-time
implementation in high-performance computing systems, such as radar, while still
producing accurate results that compare favorably to traditional methods. A case study
involving a simulated air traffic control scenario with multiple aircraft trajectories
demonstrates the significant time advantages of the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm over conventional autonomous factor analysis techniques.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering methods tailored for the development of video games. The rapidly evolving nature of the software industry, particularly the gaming sector, poses significant challenges to traditional requirements engineering approaches. This chapter examines requirements engineering techniques specifically designed to handle the unique demands of the gaming industry and highlights the importance of involving end-users and applying creative problem-solving methods. This discussion is illustrated with real-world applications and case studies from the industry.

This paper investigates the integration of differential privacy (DP) with machine learning, focusing on its application in securing the training process and preventing information leaks. We identify a key limitation of current DP-based learning algorithms, which struggle to optimize performance due to an abundance of hyperparameters. To rectify this issue, we propose a novel method for efficiently tuning these parameters in the context of DP. Our approach is straightforward to implement and significantly reduces the hyperparameter landscape for both convolutional neural networks and fully connected networks. By employing a variation of Bayesian optimization, which incorporates differential privacy, we minimize the number of required evaluations and shorten the tuning process. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, which we name DP-HPT, by achieving up to an 8-fold reduction in assessment evaluations and matching security properties. Moreover, we show that our method also enhances model accuracy, particularly for tasks where the data distribution is not Gaussian.
A strategy is outlined for analyzing boolean subalgebras of the algebra of all involutions on a given set, with specific research results addressing algebras defined by certain operation symbols.

The Euclid telescope will significantly influence nearly all astronomical research in the coming decade, yet its potential is only limited by the NISP camera's performance. To fully utilize its potential, the NISP must achieve optimal sensitivity and precise control over systematic errors. Assessing the impact of read noise on the NISP's measurement accuracy and precision is the focus of this study. A simulated Euclid science dataset was used to examine the impact of read noise correlation on the NISP's performance, examining factors like cosmic ray rejection, the readout sequence, and the impact on the data. The study found that one-dimensional read-out correlations improved the depth of a flux measurement by 0.35 dB, whereas random read noise had less impact, resulting in minimal differences in the depth. The beneficial effect of correlated read noise was primarily confined to shallow measurements. The optimal configuration of the NISP's correlated read noise pattern to minimize the flux measurement's depth loss is also discussed. The proposed analysis has direct implications for the full NISP dataset analysis in coming years.

To comprehensively understand stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis, we must identify any gaps in our knowledge of chemical patterns. In this study, we analyzed a section of the Milky Way's disk using 31,436 stars from the APOGEE-2 program, focusing on four regions of composition. We used a statistical model to break down the galaxy's population into distinct groups based on their properties, and found that two main groups explained 95% of the data in two of the regions. However, even with this high level of explanation, distinct composition patterns emerged when looking at specific elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, suggesting that these patterns may be significant in our understanding of the galaxy's history. The explanation ratio with remaining abundances was significantly lower at roughly 30%, which leaves a significant amount of information that chemical cartography aims to decipher. Additionally, we examined the accuracy of our data and the influence of observational errors, as well as the reliability of our statistical analysis. Ultimately, this research highlights the immense potential of using large spectroscopic surveys to create a detailed chemical map of our galaxy.

During the COVID-19 pandemic in China, a widespread panic over a digital rumor known as "Lion Dance Cats" was observed in 2020. This study delves into the spread of this rumor by combining theories of information dissemination and the small-world model. It assesses the rumor's spread and the conditions under which it may decline, taking into consideration the varying transmissibility and impact of the rumor on susceptible individuals. Key findings include: (1) higher transmissibility facilitates the decline of the rumor; (2) the scale and frequency of information dissemination accelerate its spread; and (1) more frequent dissemination in an small-world environment leads to quicker decline. Additionally, the study offers policy suggestions to control the spread of pandemics and rumors effectively.

The Fornax3D Consortium is establishing a comprehensive database and set of tools to study objects within the Fornax cluster, with a focus on the entire population of nebulae and galaxies, particularly in the ultraviolet to visible spectrum. Located at a moderate distance of 63 megaparsecs, the Fornax cluster provides an ideal laboratory for research, with a rich variety of stellar populations in galaxies, as well as numerous planetary nebulae as tracers of recent stellar evolution. Although previous studies on the Fornax cluster have been conducted, a comprehensive exploration of the cluster using the entire width/height of the Virgo overlay has not yet been done. To accelerate our understanding of the cluster, we are developing the entire population of planetary nebulae in two major galaxy targets, NGC 1399 and NGC 1404, through a thorough spectral analysis. By conducting observations of entire spectra of planetary nebulae within these galaxies, we can derive precise distances through the "H-beta + [O III]5007" and "TRD5007" techniques. As result, we are able to accurately measure the distance to the cluster at 61.8 megaparsecs, with a 10 percent error margin.

Processing high-volume data streams in real-time is the focus of recent research.
Depending on the complexity of the processing task, researchers have developed
various solutions: enhanced traditional database systems, specialized stream
processing frameworks, or task-specific adapters. The majority of these solutions
are designed for specific needs and can't handle a wide range of processing tasks
on highVelocity streams effectively. To tackle this limitation, we introduce a
new stream processing framework called LifeFlow, which can efficiently handle
various processing tasks on highVelocity streams. LifeFlow achieves this by
breaking down stream data into smaller, manageable lives of vertices and
processing them in a fine-grained manner. To optimize performance, LifeFlow has
developed a set of accelerators that utilize the characteristics of modern computer
architectures, such as multi-core processors and high-speed memory. The results of
the experiments show that LifeFlow outperforms existing stream processing
frameworks and even general-purpose systems in executing benchmark and real-world
applications. Compared to Breeze, one of the existing frameworks, LifeFlow is
2.4 to 5.7 times faster in typical workflows, and when integrated with Doris, a
multi-purpose database system, LifeFlow still performs better in end-to-end
benchmarks by 1.5 to 2.7 times.

We follow the standard approach to define and investigate the properties of a specific type of curve in a semi-Riemannian space, called a timelike Bertrand curve, which lies in a 3-dimensional submanifold and is curve-torsion dependent. Furthermore, we provide a specific form of the curve's equation and an example of a timelike Bertrand curve. We also establish that a timelike Bertrand curve cannot be a helix in certain dimensionally specific ways and that the curve must be an integral curve of a symmetric (1,1)-tensor for it to be a Bertrand curve, ultimately showing that such a tensor is always trace-free. Finally, we examine how this holds true for timelike curves in specific semi-Riemannian spaces, such as the pseudo-sphere and hyperbolic spaces.

The choice of loss function in a classification model is crucial, yet the underlying theory remains poorly understood. Although the cross-entropy loss is widely used, other options like the Hamming loss exist. So far, there's been little research comparing different loss functions in the context of classification. This paper investigates how different loss functions affect a classification model's performance and output, using a range of classification networks and datasets. We found that different loss functions can yield significant variations in both model accuracy and the types of categories produced, with the effect being particularly pronounced on smaller datasets. Moreover, replacing the cross-entropy loss with the Hamming loss during training resulted in substantial differences in model performance and output when evaluated against the originally trained models.

This research paper addresses the stabilization of Navier-Stokes equations using boundary feedback controllers, specifically full-state controllers applied to boundary subregions. We have proven that linear feedback controllers can be effectively used to achieve asymptotic stability for weak solutions within $H^{2+\alpha,\alpha}$ spaces. Furthermore, it is shown that non-linear feedback controllers can provide stability in specific Sobolev spaces for initial conditions and guarantee global stability for weak solutions. It is also demonstrated that boundary feedback controllers considered here have the advantage of being easily implementable and energy-efficient.

This research employs viscous mechanical simulations to analyze how crystalline patterns form and evolve in the mechanical fusible polymer model under various types of stress. By applying the same parameters to these simulations, we examine the impact of geometry and applied stress on the resulting microstructure. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for predicting polymer microstructure in the elastoplastic state, demonstrating that the orientation of formed branches within a shear band is governed by the principal stress direction. Consequently, complex branching structures within shear bands can be controlled and manipulated.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on triplet Cooper pairs in nematic superconductors, we used the Ginzburg-Landau free energy to study the superconducting state in the presence of spin-up and spin-down charges. By examining the curvature of the free energy in relation to the order parameter, we determined the susceptibility of the triplet pair. Our results revealed the susceptibility of the triplet pair to diverge near the transition temperature, following similar patterns to the specific heat. Our research also revealed the possibility of distinguishing between different types of triplet pair divergence by using magnetic field.

A popular instructional method for robotics is constructivisim, where a human creates a virtual robot that solves a task and transfers the solution to a physical robot. This approach overcomes the limitations of imitation learning, which demands extensive data collection from the physical robot. Researchers are now exploring various implementations of constructivisim, including using a simulated robot for more efficient training and data gathering, or using multiple physical robots to reduce the burden of data collection. This survey examines the properties required for constructivisim learning methods, including their ability to handle different types of constructive feedback, states, actions, and states in a realistic environment. The survey classifies and compares algorithms based on their reliance on constructive feedback and states in a simulated environment. The paper also discusses the advantages of constructivisim in practice and identifies areas in which research is still needed.

Difference Differential Continuous Phase Modulation (DCPM) detection techniques, traditionally non-coherent, are analyzed and improved in this paper. A novel differential detection method is proposed which introduces a two-symbol delay, addressing the limitation of conventional schemes that incur performance losses due to interference from the adjacent rear adjacent symbol. This proposed method outperforms conventional non-coherent detection methods and demonstrates comparable results to coherent detection. Simulations show that the proposed scheme yields a result that is 0.3dB better than conventional non-coherent detection and 0.2dB better than coherent detection at a bit error rate of 10^-5 for $\mathcal{H}$-mapping, utilizing 2T delay in comparison to 1T for conventional schemes.

Our research uses advanced computer simulations to analyze how core-collapse supernovae work, specifically in binary systems involving stars and their companions. We've discovered that the dynamics of these explosions can produce black holes in a wide range of masses, some as low as 2.8 solar masses. The presence of a companion star can also lead to the formation of direct-collapse binaries, where the star collapses into another star of the same type. This process can create optimal conditions for future collisions between the newly formed black hole and the star, producing gravitational waves with specific characteristics. If detected, such events could provide valuable information for identifying neutron-star mergers and their associated electromagnetic signals.

Evaluating the compressibility of thermal quantum thermal systems as they approach absolute zero, our research indicates that quantum potential plays a compressing role, effectively counteracting the systems' inherent expansivity.

Disentangled image encoding produces realistic synthetic data useful for tasks like rain simulation and removal, yet its potential in forming artificial precipitation has been underexplored. Another issue we identified is that current discrete cosine transform-based methods struggle to remove real-world rain due to signal losses. To address these problems, we propose a novel approach that both creates and removes rain in images. Our method involves two main components: first, a discrete cosine transform-based encoder learns to separate rain from scene elements, and second, a reverse encoder generates real precipitation and clear scenes free of rain. Disentangled rain separation enhances the quality of the formed rain, while our innovative encoding method boosts the performance of rain removal. We thoroughly test our method on public datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques through comprehensive evaluations.

One prominent global optimization strategy is cluster ranking, which leverages
user feedback to identify the most effective parameters in a generalized linear
model. The standard approach involves presenting users with ranked lists of elements
from different clusters and obtaining their preferences. While effective, this
procedure is extensively computationally demanding. We propose a more efficient
method, called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking, by allowing users to select
subclusters that share similar outcomes and visualize them. This alternative
reduces the initial parameter range and utilizes both user preferences and
data-driven information to refine the most suitable parameters of the model more
quickly than traditional techniques. Our experimental results show that our
method significantly outperforms the standard approach, requiring substantially
fewer rounds to reach convergence and outperforms it in accuracy.

The failure of topological and set-theoretic approaches to fully grasp the continuum issue has led to the suggestion that an alternative framework, such as that of panrelationalism, be explored. Under this new perspective, the focus shifts away from properties of the real number system and instead emphasizes the relationship between rational and irrational numbers within the real number system. We propose the development of a topological companion framework and present an initial topological relation theory. This new theory may offer a fresh approach to recovering the continuity property of the real number system.

This study on the Q-curvature problem in Euclidean space^n requires a specific condition for a smooth function u, namely that it approaches the constant 1 at a large distance from the origin. We have a formula for a bounded region in space^n, which connects the chiral Milnor class to a variation of the Q-integral, and this connection helps us find constraints for possible values of the Q-curvature, and also for conformal geometry in spaces that look like Euclidean space^n.

This research is an examination of how a modified version of the Five Factor Framework of character can predict an individual's propensity to engage with illegal substances. An adaptation of this framework, specifically designed for youth, is analyzed to assess its ability to measure personality traits and characterize a comprehensive assessment tool. An initial survey was administered to 597 university students to evaluate the survey's validity and reliability. Findings revealed that the survey's five facets - openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism - are supported, yet openness displays a split into two distinct areas of experience and personal development. A subsequent survey involving 353 university students and 213 high school students revealed that involvement with illegal substances, whether mild, moderate, or severe, is reliably predicted by character as outlined by the five framework framework. Specifically, students displaying heightened levels of neuroticism and low conscientiousness are found to have a greater likelihood of experiencing illegal substance use.

If-then rules constitute a widely used and effective form of Machine Readable Knowledge, though they suffer from issues like redundancy and inconsistency due to their human-generated nature. These shortcomings hinder their use in forting the basis for inference between them. To address this, we've created ATOMIC, an atlas of machine common knowledge that refines an initial set of if-then rules through the collaboration of humans and automated systems to enable reliable inter-symbolic inference. ATOMIC leverages neural models to derive high-quality neural rules from vast amounts of training data which, when combined with human verification and inter-symbolic inference, result in a high-quality explicit knowledge base. Moreover, our framework allows for the addition of symbolic facts and rules to enhance the performance of neural networks and bridges the gap between neural and symbolic AI. For the task of Natural Language Inference Classification, our method surpasses current SOTA performances, improving accuracy by 22 comparisons with 3 baseline models using 50k human-confirmed facts and 10k DeNeRALized rules.

To handle the limitations of current noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers,
our approach integrates QHHL into a variational hybrid classical-quantum framework
for optimizing objectives under constraints, specifically focusing on portfolio
selection and optimization. By replacing certain matrix operations in the HHL
algorithm with variational ones, NISQ-HHL is created as an optimized version
of NISQ-HHL, taking into account the constraints imposed by quantum hardware.
Our in-depth computational tests for portfolio optimization utilize NISQ-HHL and
NISQ-HQL, comparing their performance to variational variational hybrid classical
methods, revealing that NISQ-HHL and NISQ-HQL outperform variational approaches
for real-world data on a onetime, non-iterative basis.

A novel multi-modal training method called speech-text driven bidirectional focus is introduced. It involves pre-training an end-to-end model that integrates two separate models: a text-to-speech generation model and a speech-to-text recognition model. By training them jointly, the text-to-speech model learns to generate high-quality audio that corresponds to the target language, while the speech-to-text model focuses on accurately transcribing the generated audio. This joint training approach allows the two models to support each other, resulting in improved performance on both speech synthesis and recognition tasks.

We successfully applied the proposed method to multiple datasets including Librispeech, Speech-2-Text and Common Voice. The method achieved significant performance gains compared to the baseline models. Specifically, we achieved a 47% reduction in word error rate (WER) when using a multi-speaker corpus, and a 27% improvement when training on a single speaker's data. The results indicate that the proposed method is highly effective and can lead to substantial performance improvements when working with multi-modal data.

This research investigates the asymptotic behavior of mean cross section width along directed boundary paths in a planar domain as the number of steps increases. It also examines the relationship between this mean cross section width and the geometry of the boundary in Dirichlet problems.

This study precisely determines the expected value and variance of the initial numbers chosen in a uniform parking process as it grows, and also demonstrates that certain second moments converge to specific values. Furthermore, this implies that the initial numbers from the process closely match the values predicted by their corresponding probability distributions. We further examine the behavior of these moments in non-asymptotic scenarios and provide numerical validation for our theoretical findings.

The critical current of superconducting circuits is influenced by both quantum and classical charges. In this study, the behavior of superconducting nanowires is investigated as the gate-induced charging energy in Josephson junctions is modified beyond a threshold, causing their transition from insulating to superconducting states. The critical current in this study is found to oscillate as the number of Cooper pairs participating in the Josephson coupling changes, which indicates that the charging energy is successfully controlling a quantum variable. However, the nature of control is distinct from the standard single-electron switching observed in normal state tunneling transistors. The coherent quantum behavior is distinguished from insulating state humps and results in increased critical currents, which may have an application in developing high-performance superconducting circuits.

The red dwarf star GJ 229 was discovered to be accompanied by a tiny, dark planet GJ 229B in 1995, the companion's spectrum underwent in-depth analysis with several telescopes and the SMAP code with which the initial atmospheric composition prediction was made. Since its inception in 2007, the SMAP code has since been upgraded and replaced with the APOLLO code with which the final atmospheric prediction was done. A detailed comparison between observational and theoretical spectra enabled by high-accuracy laboratory data for molecular carbon monoxide revealed significant differences between the two codes primarily attributed to the treatment of molecular line transitions. The apodization and least-squares methods employed by the APOLLO code yielded the most accurate atmospheric prediction which also matches the visible and near-infrared observations made with the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck I telescope. The research further demonstrates the ability of the APOLLO code to accurately predict the atmospheric composition of T-dwarfs such as GJ 229B and which now serves as which now serves a useful benchmark for the efficient spectral analysis of astrophysical objects within the scope of the fourth generation Chinese 5-meter telescope FAST.

Studies of the quark-gluon fluid's viscosity to entropy ratio suggest that its profound inelastic scattering plays a minimal role in determining this value. Consequently, our work delves into the question of whether the high-inelasticity threshold is genuinely required or if our understanding of inelastic scattering dynamics is flawed. To examine this, we utilize relativistic hydrodynamics to derive an explicit formula for the shear viscosity, and we observe that the contribution from highly inelastic scattering can have a negative influence, thereby challenging the necessity of this requirement.

Predicting human movement based on perspective-based data is crucial in
shaping safer and more engaging virtual environments. This task is particularly
complex due to the noisy and incomplete nature of perspective motion data, which
includes significant variations in human movement patterns that often lead to
ambiguous future states. This paper presents a novel approach, DRAN, to address
this challenge. DRAN utilizes a unique two-part encoding system that maps
perspective human movement into both ordinal and continuous time series data
series. This allows for a more stable and reliable analysis of perspective
human movement in the subsequent moments. By leveraging the benefits of both
time series processing methods, our approach ensures more accurate and diverse
perspective human movement forecasts. Experimental results indicate that DRAN
outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and
variability when predicting perspective human movement.

Valence forces acting across different electron shells are significant yet not fully understood, particularly the interaction between d and f electrons in transition and rare earth compounds. Despite being overlooked in most standard electronic structure models, such as the Hubbard model, this inter-shell interaction could be crucial to unravelling the complex behaviour and electronic properties of these materials. A key challenge in assessing its impact has been the difficulty in directly measuring this inter-orbital coupling. Through X-ray spectroscopic analysis and theoretical modeling, researchers have now observed inter-orbital correlation effects and determined the magnitude of the coupling in rare earth ddf systems. The degree of these correlation effects serves as a clear i.ndicator of the inter-orbital coupling strength, which was found to vary between different compounds but could not be explained by other known forces, allowing for the first direct assessment of the inter-orbital coupling constant through this investigation.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments at the FAIR facility in Germany and the J-PARC laboratory in Japan, has always been difficult to identify due to its long production-decay timeline. To improve the identification of this particle researchers now aim to create it in a bound state within nuclei at these facilities. To aid them in this endeavor, we have conducted a theoretical analysis using a quark model to predict the characteristic signs of the excited Ω-baryon state. Our results show how the constituent quark masses, especially the mass related to the s-quark coupling, affect the masses and composition of the ground and excited states of 1-quark excitation type. To make these signs more relatable, quark spin-spin interactions between quarks have been linked to their constituent quark masses for both singlet and octet spin states. By applying a linear quark path approach, we have also explored the impact of s-quark interaction on the baryon sign patterns. In adroit circumstances, we found that the spin-orbit interaction can be expressed as the product of two distinct factors. To quark excitation, we have examined the impact of the s-quark interaction on baryon signs and found it to be significantly relatable to the pattern produced by light quark interaction. These outcomes are displayed in tabular form, while the s-quark interaction in some instances has also been connected to

Public spaces pose a significant risk for the rapid transmission of respiratory infections due to frequent close contacts among individuals. To effectively contain the spread of disease on urban public transit systems, researchers are investigating the benefits of applying isolation strategies by creating networked isolation networks. An analytical model has been developed to evaluate public transit vs. isolated transmission scenarios and how these dynamics change with varying levels of network connectivity. The model takes into account the size of the transmission or isolation network, as well as its level of modularity. Results indicate that even low levels of network separation can significantly reduce the speed at which infections spread, with highly disconnected clusters offering even greater benefits. The model is also applicable to other contexts, such as enhancing privacy in office environments during times of heightened infection risk. Using real-world data from the COVID-19 spread on Los Angeles buses during the 2014 flu season, the model estimates that up to 80% of riders may be infected by end of season and benefits of isolation networks include up to 40% in increased reach and reduced time for the infection to spread to a maximal number of people.

Quantum electrodynamics predicts subtle effects in the vacuum such as light scattering and the splitting of polarized light during the diffraction of electromagnetic waves, which are difficult to detect due to their minute magnitudes. However, the possibility of amplifying these effects through the use of high-intensity lasers has been an area of interest. Various proposed methods involving extremely powerful lasers have so far failed to detect these phenomena. This failure indicates significant challenges that any successful detection method must overcome. We analyze the conditions and constraints on the detection of QED vacuum diffraction and double refraction, highlighting the importance of minimizing noise and controlling experimental setups. To facilitate future attempts, we suggest specific technical requirements and potential detection schemes aimed at distinguishing quantum split beams from classical phenomena caused by scattering and refractive effects.

This note presents an innovative technique to swiftly determine the point coordinate
information for highly symmetric shapes like the 600-cell, 24-cell, and 120-cell.
The method's efficacy has been verified by employing it to list the vertex
coordinates of the 600-cell.

We revisit the reappearing key concept, originally explored by G. G.
Stinson and T. van de Graaf in 2000, in relation to synchronizing
channels and data storage systems. Our analysis yields two main
advancements. Firstly, we refine the original criteria for an n
repeating encryption and an n
sync device to be functional. Secondly, we establish the original and
modified requirements as equivalent. A key difference between the two sets
of requirements lies in their treatment of incorrect inputs. An essential
component of our proof involves the development of a new sync device, called
the universal sync device, which can recover from errors caused by
tampering. This has implications for a synergent decryption process, which we
examine in detail.

Physical layer security, an emerging authentication and secret sharing method, relies on unique environmental characteristics to distinguish friendly and hostile devices. While existing in RF environments in RF environments offers high uniqueness, it requires prior knowledge of a shared secret, such as a calibration code, which compromises the security of the method by making it vulnerable to attacks from malicious devices with access to the code. From a security standpoint, the ability of a device with access to the code to replicate the physical layer characteristics is significantly lower than that of a device with unlimited access to the code. Therefore, although not commonly used in RF systems, RFS requires prior knowledge of a shared secret.

In contrast, we show the feasibility of a verification system, operating in the audio frequency range, that does not require a shared secret to differentiate between friendly and hostile devices. Our fully hardware-based system achieves a bit error rate of as low as 0.013 under noisy conditions, allowing for a secure match between two devices with no prior knowledge of a shared secret and detection of a malicious device at a 87 % bit error rate. Moreover, our system can also be used to generate a shared code between two devices with a low rate of failing to generate a match (0.125), even when subjected to an attack (0.875).

Our findings also reveal that two devices can be securely identified and distinguished from a malicious device by analyzing the frequency components of their audio fingerprints. Our observation that each device modifies

We investigate the flat-band surface plasmons in isolated and stacked TSDCs, and provide a flat-band plasmonic frequency formula for them. Plots of the asymptotic flat-band plasmonic frequencies in monolayers and magic-angle doubly stacked layers are supplied for various TSDC types. Notably, the Assembled Flat-Band Plasmonic Spectra diagram can predict the flat-band plasmonic behavior in magic-angle doubly stacked TSDCs from monolayer data. This association reveals that certain magic-angle doubly stacked TSDCs exhibit identical flat-band plasmons with their single-layer counterparts. These equivalencies include flat-band plasmons in double CVD-stacked MoS₂ with that in single-layer MoS₂ and in magic-angle stacked WS₂ with magic-angle MoS₂.

This research paper expands the study of Ricci solitons on Sasakian manifolds by focusing on the properties of nearly conformal Ricci solitons. We provide the fundamental equations defining these solitons and demonstrate that, on a 3-dimensional Sasakian manifold, the potential function being constant implies that the soliton is equivalent to a gradient conformal Ricci soliton. Additionally, we demonstrate that on a Ricci flat Sasakian manifold, the potential function being harmonic leads to the conclusion that the manifold is isospectral.

In systems involving hot stars and massive magnetic fields, stellar winds and planetary magnetospheres significantly influence w-stars and red giants, as well as celestial bodies that generate winds via magnetic fields. These effects are even more pronounced in these systems than in cases where the star emits primarily via absorption of light. Additionally, the magnetospheres of planets and their surrounding magnetic fields shape their environments and can protect them from incoming winds and magnetized waves. These structures determine the emission of non-thermal radiation, trap plasma, and create localized magnetic fields that emit intense bursts of thermal and non-thermal waves. On Earth, the interaction between the solar wind and the ionosphere creates the upper layers of the atmosphere and influences the planet's magnetosphere. This system is well understood and even allows for intentional communication via ionospheric reflections. Furthermore, similar phenomena occur on other celestial bodies, such as moons and planets with dense atmospheres, where magnetospheres can be compressed into intense bursts of radiation near their surfaces.

Spin-orbit proximity effects result in strong coupling between the spin-split d-bands of a ferromagnetic material and the split s-p bands of an adjacent non-magnetic layer. This can lead to enhanced spin-splitting and a large anomalous Hall effect in the non-magnetic material. We studied the spin-orbit proximity influence in an epitaxial Bi/Co multilayer consisting of several Co units on top of a thick Bi substrate. By altering the Bi thickness, we were able to measure the changes in spin-split energy and anomalous Hall effect in the Co layers. Our experiments revealed that spin-orbit proximity coupling leads to significant spin-splitting in the Bi/Co multilayer, with the magnitude of the splitting governed by the Co layers' scattering at the Bi interface. Notably, spin-orbit proximity influence was found to be larger in the Bi/Co multilayer compared to both a Bi/single Co layer and the intrinsic properties of the Co layers.

This study presents analytical solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation, utilizing the generalized Mie-type potential in higher dimensions. A Jumarie type fractional derivative plays a key role in this analysis. Through the application of He's variational iteration method, explicit and convergent fractions of wave functions are derived for the fractional Schrödinger equation. Numerical examples and graphical illustrations demonstrate the efficacy of derived solutions.

We have developed a novel approach to improve neural network models by enforcing them to adhere to Lipschitz consistency. This method is designed to prevent the models from exploiting patterns of minimal significance, thereby ensuring that their predictions remain reliable. We theoretically prove that our approach ensures the trained neural network to possess the lowest possible Lipschitz constant, thereby providing a unique solution due to its optimality. To efficiently solve this problem, we employ the proximal gradient method by introducing a novel parameterization of the neural network. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by comparing the neural network models based on their accuracy and resistance to adversarial manipulation. Furthermore, our approach can be integrated with existing training techniques by using the non-smooth regularization property of the nuclear norm. The results indicate that the models trained with our approach exhibit significant resistance to adversarial manipulation and outperform methods like K-Net in terms of performance. We also observe that enforcing low-Lipschitz consistency enables neural networks to generalize more effectively.

Social influence in language leads to the loss of a language or the adoption of a more powerful one, ultimately leading to language extinction. In this paper, a mathematical framework is established to model the loss of a language under social pressure. A specific mechanism, the consensus update rule, is examined in the context of our model. We demonstrate that social pressure causes the majority language to be adopted by all agents within $O(\log n)$ interactions, and the network size affects the time required for this to occur. These findings are supported by simulations and experimental results performed with a real-world endangered language, Basque.

Using globally distributed telescopes, we conducted extensive observations of a highly eccentric planet, HD 80606 b, which inhibits the creation of a reliable ephemeris, even for upcoming primary events in 2025 and 2026. Comboney et al. (2023) successfully predicted orbit periastron on March 1, 2023. We carried out pre- and post-terranshot observations using multiple telescopes, adding to the successful use of the Pre-DESI, DESI-AJ, and worldwide networks. These observations revealed significant inconsistencies when compared to the previous findings. To effectively schedule observations for terrestrial chords and potentially utilize the Next Generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), we analyzed angular differential spectroscopy during the successful prediction of periastron in 2023. The angular differential spectroscopy revealed the K edge of potassium on the planetary atmosphere. The combination of traditional and very large array telescopes allowed for the measurement of radial velocity at the periastron and the determination of the orbital elements through the Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method using angular differential spectroscopy. The orbital parameters obtained indicate that another terrestrial chord primary transit will happen on August 1, 2027. Video games have made significant advancements in computer graphics and artificial intelligence over the past few decades, which have now found applications in improving human movement and rehabilitation in related fields. In the context of movement therapy and physical therapy, players can benefit from the dynamic interaction with a virtual character that mimics their motions in a playful and engaging manner. This paper delves into a system that combines a 3D virtual agent with computer-generated animation to recreate human movement in a therapy setting. By utilizing a scene of foundation gameplay, we can develop a recovery system that can be used for various purposes, including motion therapy and physical therapy. This paper also discusses the potential of this system to serve as a starting point for future research in this field.

Our research offers a variational interpretation of the phase-field approximation
introduced by Andrews and Jordan for the regularized piecewise-stiff map $\gamma$ in
the context of total variation diffusion. It proves that for a suitable choice of
parameter, the regularized functional converges to the original one as it approaches
its limit. The proof relies on the rate of convergence being similar to the previously
established result by Beirao da Costa, Jordan and Le Tallec. The study also relates
this finding to the previously demonstrated results by Ambrosio and Fusco as well as the
work by Franzoni.

We examine the Drell-Yan production of heavy quark pairs, specifically top-quarks, at hadron colliders within the framework of third-generation vector leptoquarks. These interactions can result in observable deviations from Standard Model predictions for diphoton processes and may also create noticeable differences in top-quark kinematic distributions. Although the DLL process is straightforward to analyze at leading order, next-to-leading order corrections introduce logarithmic enhancements that require careful treatment to accurately assess their impact on cross-section calculations. Such corrections are essential for comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data and for constraining the possible parameters of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory.

Advanced medical imaging modalities such as PET enable the non-invasive visualization and remote monitoring of metabolic processes and physiological functions within the human body. Due to increased scanning demands driven by the proliferation of mobile devices, patients may be required to undergo prolonged PET sessions, which can be uncomfortable and unproductive. One potential solution involves reducing the radiotracer dose to shorten scanning time; however, low-dose PET images often suffer from noisy images and inaccurate diagnoses as a result. Our research focuses on developing reduced-dose PET imaging techniques utilizing neural networks trained to minimize uncertainty across multiple outcomes such as diagnosis prediction, disease staging, and treatment planning. Our proposed framework leverages the real-data distribution to train resilient neural network modules that minimize both expected risk and K-largest outcomes, allowing for more reliable data processing even when faced with altered data distributions resulting from reduced PET dose. By employing a careful selection of neural network modules and applying cost controls, we can train our system to reduce risk while maintaining resilience against the significant increase in noise associated with reduced-dose PET images. Our proposed framework achieves improved performance compared to existing methods, demonstrating superior results in various medical applications such as diagnosis prediction, disease staging, and treatment planning based on reduced-dose PET images.

Multi-tenant SaaS systems provide users with multiple features, features that can be customized by individual tenants, but are also visible to other tenants and potentially insecure. To overcome this, we propose a new system called "Fully Customizable and Secure Software as a Service" (FCSSS), which allows for the safe customization of applications in these environments. Our proposal, based on confidential computing technology, provides a level of security that is missing from existing SaaS systems, but also addresses the performance issues that often arise from these security measures. In the context of code compilation, we developed a new method called "Secure and Individualized Code Compilation" (ICSSC), which is supported by a new tool called Sanctus. This tool is optimized for speed, overcoming the typical performance drawbacks associated with security-focused code compilation. We evaluated Sanctus and found that it can be up to five times slower than existing systems, but in some cases, it can actually be three times faster.

This paper investigates the compatibility of centering theory with contemporary deep learning frameworks, specifically within the context of neural coreference resolution systems.
By analyzing and adapting key aspects of the centering framework – namely, the concepts of focal point, structural framework, and theoretical limitations – this study seeks to enhance coreference modeling capabilities.
To verify the hypothesis that elements aligned with the centering principles can be effectively integrated into neural models, this research modifies a state-of-the-art coreference model and conducts targeted experiments using controlled sentence sets designed to assess specific centering theory functions.
The results show significant advancements in accuracy, efficiency, and consistency when the centering framework is incorporated, confirming the utility of the centering theory concepts within the coreference domain and paving the way for further exploration of cognitive-inspired models.

This paper explores parameterized methods for two related problems in graph theory: upward planarity and bi-up planarity of directed graphs. Specifically, we are looking at situations where certain subgraphs are pre-positioned in the plane while other vertices need to be added. For the first situation, we have a graph with a Hamiltonian subgraph that needs to be made upward planary by adding a directed path and a set of forward edges. We have found that this problem is easy to solve if the number of new edges is a fixed size, but difficult for other cases. For the second situation, we have a subgraph with every vertex connected to two other vertices by opposite-direction edges, and we are looking to make this graph bi-up planary with more edges that have the same opposite direction. We have found that this problem is difficult even with a single additional edge that connects to each of the fixed vertices.

Custom frameworks are popular choices for training machine learning models due to their versatility, but they also present a barrier to entry for new contributors who must manually replicate the build process. This process can be streamlined by creating a setup automation script that streamlines framework configuration. This proposal outlines key components for such a script, using OpenCV as a practical example, and highlights the broader benefits for the computer vision community.

In the Intervals framework for Measurable Space, we've developed a new concept called the Operator Expansion Coefficient, whichintertwines various operator expansions within the same measure space and allows for a deeper exploration of their relationships. By applying this idea, we've discovered a fascinating connection between Gram-Schmidt expansion and the Hadamard-Lebesgue operator expansion, revealing that the former can be seen as an infinitesimal version of the latter. This discovery has profound implications in the field of Probability Theory, particularly in understanding the integration by parts process.

Using supervised machine learning models to predict coordinates based on WiFi signal strength requires a large and high-quality dataset for training. To minimize human input, a new approach is proposed in this paper where the neural network generates proxy data for missing coordinates and assesses the closeness of these predictions to actual data. To further improve the model, the use of distance metrics such as MSE and MSE-root in the loss function during optimization is explored, along with the impact of including extra features (e.g., time of day) and different optimization strategies.

An alternative concept to the black hole, known as the black star, is explored with a self-holding photon sphere around the extreme compact object. A suitable sleeve for this photon sphere in the form of an equatorial Dyson shell is studied in this work. By applying first-order stability criteria and examining small perturbations in radius and thickness, the stability of this Dyson shell is determined. Additionally, energy conditions in the form of null, energy, dominant and cosmological are investigated to understand the physical behavior of the black star. A graphical analysis is performed to visualize the photon sphere, and a numerical evaluation in a graph form is done to verify the stability of the Dyson shell. Furthermore, a comparison with observations of S2 star and G2 in the galaxy center near Milky Way is done to obtain the mass of the supermassive object. It is found from this investigation that the photon sphere will exist at approximately 3.0001 times the Schwarzschild radius and the Dyson shell around the black hole like object of the mass of $4.153\times 10^{39}$ kg will be stable.

In a cloud computing context, the failure to meet promised service quality in SLA indicates a breach. Determining an accurate Breach Threshold (BT) is crucial, as it distinguishes acceptable service breaches from unacceptable ones. An inaccurate BT determination results in unnecessary cost increases or unrecovered losses due to over- or under-compensation. We introduce the concept of using peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to identify BT in a distributed manner, where multiple users with varying needs collaborate to find the most effective BT and are compensated for their input by others who are paying for the best BT. This cooperative yet competitive approach is called the SLA Breach Identification Market (SBIM). We model the user behavior and optimal strategies in SBIM, and design an algorithm to efficiently implement the market. The results indicate that SBIM can produce the best BT while minimizing communication requirements between users.

The possibility of utilizing regenerative beam transport between discards allows for greater flexibility in beam handling, particularly at high energies. However, beam fragmentation instabilities pose a challenge that must be addressed, especially when the beam current is significant. This study investigates the impact of energy recovery linac (ERL) beam configuration on beam fragmentation instabilities, specifically in relation to a high-energy, short-bunch (2.7 GHz, 125 picoseconds) beam line. By systematically varying the beam fill pattern and position within the linac, the study aims to identify the influence these factors have on the instability's beam fragmentation behavior. Furthermore, by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental measurements of beam halo growth, the study seeks to deepen our understanding of beam halo formation mechanisms.

Integrating high-rate scintillator detectors into the neutron flux measurement framework is the critical limitation in present-forward heavy-ion physics experiments. This research presents an innovative 3D-projection scintillator design that effectively mitigates this limitation, particularly in neutron cross-section studies. An analytical model has been developed to explain the scintillator behavior under neutron bombardment, considering CH composition, the nuclear recoil and proton emission ranges influenced by neutron reactions, as well as the particle range differences which may lead to significant energy losses. Based on this analytical model, a detailed simulation framework has been created utilizing GEANT4, revealing the 3D distribution of neutron and proton emission, as well as proton capture on activated scintillator material. This simulation reveals a dominant proton distribution in specific spatial areas, enabling the implementation of optimized detection strategies. Furthermore, the proposed detector design exhibits remarkable robustness, with only a 10% variation in proton-electron signal ratio under high neutron flux rates, ensuring the detector's reliability and performance.

Our primary goal remains studying how dust grains interact within protoplanetary discs, specifically in relation to the temperature changes as they rise. In this work, we further examine how the adherence forces between dust and surface interact in relation to temperature changes, in order to determine the conditions under which dust processing occurs. This involves re-evaluating the conditions present in a protoplanetary surface at rising temperatures, in comparison to the processing conditions found in a laboratory laboratory. To accomplish this, it is necessary to adapt the six solvent-free solutions originally studied by re-introducing six different hydrogen compounds to the experiments, in order to determine how the conditions under which dust grains and surfaces interact as they are exposed to increasing temperatures. The re-evaluations in the protoplanetary disc and the additional analyses in the laboratory in relation to temperature changes in relation to the experimental conditions.
